newsitem.title: INDIA: Mitsubishi eyes India auto part market.
newsitem.headline: Mitsubishi eyes India auto part market.

text.p: The Indian unit of Mitsubishi Material Corp (MMTL) said on Wednesday it was expecting to garner 30 percent of India's auto components market.
"We think we can have a market share of 30 percent in the gear and synchroniser rings sector in India in the next few years," Tahehiko Mizugai, senior managing director of MMTL, told Reuters.
He was speaking after a news conference to announce the start of a joint venture with India's Sona Steering Systems Ltd.

The joint venture, Sona-Okegawa Precision Forgings Ltd, was formed last July and is owned 45 percent by Sona Steering, 26.25 percent by Mitsubishi Materials, and 3.75 percent by Japanese trading house Mitsubishi Corp.
The remaining 25 percent will be taken up by investment banks, although details have yet to be decided, company officials said.
They said the plant, which is being built near New Delhi, would produce precision-forged differential gears and synchroniser rings for manual transmissions.
"If the investment by banks doesn't work out, we may decide to go public after some months," Surinder Kapur, managing director of Sona Steering Systems Ltd, told reporters.
The joint venture is expected to cost 600 million rupees ($17 million). The plant would be completed by 1997 and production would begin in April 1998, company officials said.
"We are targeting a sale of 3.2 million pieces in the first year of production of which one million will be synchroniser rings and 2.2 million will be gears," Kapur said.
Kapur said the auto components manufactured by the joint venture would cater for light commercial vehicles, tractors, jeeps, cars and vans.
"We will be seeking a yen loan to the extent of 210 million rupees for (part financing) the joint venture," he said.

The turnover of the joint venture was expected to be around 250 million rupees in the first year and go up to 800-1000 million rupees by 2000, Kapur said. A company statement said the company in future would diversify into products such as clutches and sprockets for agricultural equipment and cars.
It would also make copper alloy forgings for oil hydraulic equipment, nickel based alloy forgings for aerospace engines and forgings for air-conditioner parts.
Mizugai said in the past several years Indian government policy had become open and transparent. "As a result, establishing joint ventures has become easy," he said.
He said many Indian companies were keen to set up joint ventures with MMTL to manufacture auto components but nothing had been finalised.
